scenes.heading: Chromosomes and karyotypes
scenes.sub: How your DNA is packed, counted and checked
scenes.say: Almost every cell in your body carries a full set of DNA instructions, packed into chromosomes. Doctors can check them with a picture called a karyotype. Let's see how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: An album has tracks; a track can have different versions
scenes.science: A chromosome has genes; a gene can have different alleles
scenes.breaks: Songs are just played. A gene is read by the cell to make a product, usually a protein.
scenes.say: Think of your genome as a music library. Each chromosome is an album, and each gene is a track. Its locus is the track number. An allele is a different version of that track, like an acoustic version. You get two copies of each album, one from mum and one from dad.

scenes.heading: Don't mix these up

left.title: Homologous chromosomes
points: One from mum, one from dad

scenes.say: Homologous chromosomes are like two editions of the same recipe book: one from mum, one from dad. Same genes, but maybe different alleles. Sister chromatids are identical photocopies, joined at the centromere. Count the centromeres: one centromere means one chromosome.

scenes.heading: Your chromosome numbers
points: 22 pairs of autosomes + XX or XY
scenes.say: Your body cells are diploid, with forty-six chromosomes: twenty-two pairs of autosomes, plus two sex chromosomes. Gametes are haploid, with twenty-three. When sperm and egg join, twenty-three plus twenty-three makes forty-six again.
scenes.caption: Your body cells are diploid, with 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes, plus two sex chromosomes. Gametes are haploid, with 23. When sperm and egg join, 23 + 23 makes 46 again.

scenes.heading: Making a karyotype
scenes.say: To make a karyotype, cells are stopped in metaphase, when chromosomes are easiest to see. They're stained to show bands. Then they're matched into pairs by size, centromere position and banding pattern. Some Cats Bark. Pairs one to twenty-two go first, then the sex chromosomes.
scenes.caption: To make a karyotype, cells are stopped in metaphase, when chromosomes are easiest to see. They're stained to show bands. Then they're matched into pairs by size, centromere position and banding pattern. Some Cats Bark. Pairs 1 to 22 go first, then the sex chromosomes.

scenes.heading: Read the karyotype
scenes.question: A karyotype has 21 normal pairs of autosomes, three copies of chromosome 21, and an X and a Y. What does it show?
lines: XY, so male; an extra 21 is trisomy
scenes.say: This karyotype has twenty-one normal pairs of autosomes, three copies of chromosome twenty-one, and an X and a Y. Count them: forty-seven. The sex chromosomes show it's male. The extra chromosome twenty-one is trisomy. So it's written forty-seven, X Y, plus twenty-one. That's Down syndrome.
scenes.caption: This karyotype has 21 normal pairs of autosomes, three copies of chromosome 21, and an X and a Y. Count them: 47. The sex chromosomes show it's male. The extra chromosome 21 is trisomy. So it's written 47,XY,+21. That's Down syndrome.

points: Alleles are versions of a gene
scenes.say: Quick recap. Alleles are versions of a gene. Body cells are diploid and gametes are haploid. Karyotypes pair chromosomes by size, centromere and banding. And aneuploidy, like trisomy or monosomy, usually comes from non-disjunction in meiosis. Now try the practice questions!
